questions.question:
**Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom/phrase.**

Work out
questions.solution:
The correct answer is "**Exercise or develop a plan".**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The phrasal verb "**work out**" has the following meanings:

 
• To exercise, either in general or by targeting a specific part of the body.
 
• To develop or refine something, such as a plan, strategy, etc.
 
 
• **Example**: *Rohan's plan to spoil his rival's dance performance didn't **work out**__.*
 
 

 
• We use the given idiom in both a literal sense as well as a phrasal verb.
 
• When used **literally**, we mean work out as a physical exercise to keep the body active.
 
• When used as a **phrasal verb**, we mean work out as a plan for a situation or scenario one is dealing with.

questions.question:
**The given sentence contains a grammatical error. Identify the segment that contains the error.**

My cousin is not like going for a walk very much.
questions.solution:
The erroneous segment is "**is not like**"

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• In the given sentence, the use of the verb "**is**" is incorrect.
 
• The verb "is" is a **stative **verb.
 
• **Stative verbs** represent a **state of being** or a condition.
 
 
• **Example**: *He **is**__** **unconscious due to the sedatives from the operation.*
 
 
 
• In the given sentence, we need to use an **action verb **since the sentence is describing an action.
 
• **Action verbs** are those verbs that describe what a person, animal, thing, or process can do.
 
• The appropriate action verb form will be '**does**'.
 
• In the given sentence, '**does**' describes what the subject of the sentence is not fond of doing.
 
• Hence, the correct answer is **option 1.**

 

**The correct sentence is**: *My cousin __**does**__** **not like going for a walk very much.*

questions.question:
**Select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select 'No substitution required'.**

She came to work __in spite of__ the heavy rain.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is "**No substitution required**"

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• Let's look at why the other given options are incorrect.
 
• In option 2, despite has the same meaning as in spite. Also, the given option is wrong because 'of' is not used after despite.
 
 
• **Example**:* She came to school **despite **being sick.*
 
 
 
• In option 3, we use 'while' to represent actions that are simultaneous. This is not suitable here.
 
 
• **Example**: *It started snowing **while **he was driving on the highway.*
 
 
 
• In option 4, we use although as a conjunction to show that the first clause is surprising.
 
 
• **Example**: *They don't talk to each other much **although **they are very good friends.*
 
 
 
• Hence, the correct answer is option 1.

 

**The correct sentence is:*** She came to work in spite of__ the heavy rain.*

* [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/9074044cf96dc1d09ca89eac99180c3d7440ade1b364d09d47931959bf693cc8.png] **__Confusion Points__***

 
• The correct usage is "**despite**" on its own, without "**of**."
 
• For example, you would say:
 
 
• "**Despite **the rain, we went for a walk."
 
 
 
• Using "**despite of"** is incorrect in standard English.
